titre: Grassmann's Law and the Dissimilation of Aspirates
accroche: In Greek, "I have grown" should double the breath of "I grow." It doesn't: a word never keeps two aspirated consonants next to each other.
contenu_vulgarise:
The Greek verb φύω, "I grow" or "I sprout," forms its perfect by reduplication: the first syllable in principle copies the root's initial consonant, as other Greek verbs do. One would expect *phephyka*. The form actually attested is πέφυκα, *pephyka*: the reduplicated consonant has lost its aspiration, while the second one kept it. The same happens with θύω, "I sacrifice": in the aorist passive, one would expect *ethythē*, and the attested form is ἐτύθη, *etythē*. In both cases, a word that should carry two neighboring aspirated consonants keeps only one, and always the second.

## A Rule, Not a Pronunciation Accident

This loss doesn't vary from word to word: it follows a systematic rule, stated in 1863 by the German mathematician and linguist Hermann Grassmann, in an article in the Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung. Grassmann shows that both Ancient Greek and Sanskrit forbid a word from carrying two aspirated consonants in two neighboring syllables: when a grammatical form would produce two, the first loses its aspiration and the second stays intact. Indian grammarians had already noticed, centuries earlier, a similar phenomenon within Sanskrit alone, without connecting it to any other language. Grassmann, for his part, shows that the same constraint runs through two distinct Indo-European languages, which strengthens the proof that they descend from a common ancestor.

## What Still Remains Debated

The rule itself has not been in dispute for a century and a half. Its theoretical description has. Two readings still compete among historical linguists: either the root originally carries two aspirates and the first one loses it, the reading favored today; or it carries only one, which shifts leftward within the word in certain contexts, as ancient Sanskrit grammarians read it. The two analyses predict almost always the same attested forms; they differ only on edge cases, such as the total absence, in Greek, of roots that would carry an aspirate followed by a voiceless consonant within the same word.

## What This Shifts

A century and a half after Grassmann's article, the regularity he isolated is no longer questioned; how to represent it in ancient speakers' grammar still is. Joined to Grimm's law, which also governs consonants across Indo-European languages, it is part of the small number of sound laws that made it possible, consonant by consonant, to reconstruct a common ancestor for languages separated by millennia, with no text attesting to it directly.

repere.texte: Grassmann publishes his demonstration in 1863, in volume 12 of the Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung, pages 81 to 138: Ancient Greek and Sanskrit, two distinct languages, each turn out to forbid two aspirated consonants in two neighboring syllables of the same word.
repere.source: Hermann Grassmann, Zeitschrift für vergleichende Sprachforschung, vol. 12, 1863, p. 81-138

carte.punch: A Greek word never keeps two neighboring aspirates: one of them always disappears, the same one.
carte.idee: In Ancient Greek and Sanskrit, a word cannot carry two aspirated consonants in two neighboring syllables: if a grammatical form would produce two, the first loses its aspiration. Hermann Grassmann states the rule in 1863, further proof of the kinship between the two languages.

quiz.question: Why doesn't the Greek perfect of φύω ("I grow"), πέφυκα, reduplicate the root's aspirated consonant?
choix: Because Ancient Greek forbids a word from carrying two aspirated consonants in two neighboring syllables, and the first of the two loses its aspiration
Because perfect reduplication only applies to verbs whose root begins with a vowel
Because πέφυκα is a loanword from Sanskrit, which never had reduplicated aspirated consonants
Because Hermann Grassmann proposed in 1863 to simplify Ancient Greek spelling for modern readers
quiz.explication: Grassmann's law (1863) shows that Ancient Greek and Sanskrit forbid two aspirated consonants in two neighboring syllables of the same word: when a grammatical form would produce two, as here with perfect reduplication, the first loses its aspiration and the second stays intact. φύω doesn't have a vowel-initial root, πέφυκα isn't a loanword, and Grassmann describes an ancient pronunciation rule, not a spelling reform.
